title: AI in Computational Thinking Education in Higher Education: A Systematic Literature Review
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of a comprehensive overview of how artificial intelligence has been applied to computational thinking (CT) education in higher education. The authors note that although CT education has been widely discussed in K-12 settings, higher education instructors still lack a clear synthesis of AI-based initiatives, their educational benefits and challenges, the instructional strategies used, the CT components targeted, and the AI techniques employed. The review is therefore designed to map and analyze the state of the literature on AI in CT education for higher education contexts.

The study uses a systematic literature review method following a seven-step review process. The authors searched ACM and IEEE digital libraries for English-language, peer-reviewed journal and conference publications from 2017 to 2022 focused on higher education, excluding generative AI and large language model studies because the evidence base was considered too immature. From 64 initially identified publications, 18 papers were selected for full review. The analysis used open thematic qualitative content analysis to identify recurring themes related to benefits and challenges, instructional strategies, CT components, and AI methods.

The context of the reviewed studies is higher education, primarily involving university students learning CT and programming, with instructors also relevant as implementers and intended users of the review’s findings. Across the included studies, AI-supported approaches included adaptive gamification platforms, recommendation systems, predictive student models, chatbots, AR systems, social robots, and machine learning-based tools. Instructional strategies included gamification, personalized/adaptive learning, project-based learning, task-based learning, and experiential learning.

The main conclusions are that AI shows strong potential to personalize CT learning, address heterogeneous student backgrounds, improve CT knowledge and skills, and motivate engagement. At the same time, the review identifies important challenges, including risks of over-reliance on AI that may reduce creativity, difficulties in accurately modeling student competencies, and the expertise demands of developing and deploying AI-based educational tools. The authors also argue that AI is expanding the notion of CT beyond coding toward broader practices such as data analysis, digital product design, and computational empowerment. They recommend future research that broadens the publication sources and time frame, especially to include more recent work on generative AI and LLMs.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A broad category of AI-based educational systems and applications used to support computational thinking education, including adaptive games, conversational agents, recommendation systems, predictive student models, AR tools, and social robot programming environments.
identified_tools.use_case: This systematic literature review synthesized 18 higher-education studies on AI applications in computational thinking education, covering heterogeneous tools such as CTQ, GidgetML, ScratchThAI, ExposAR, predictive student modeling systems, and other AI-supported learning environments.

findings.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, AI-based initiatives were reported to support computational thinking learning by personalizing instruction, addressing heterogeneous prior backgrounds, and building CT knowledge and skills. The review highlights examples including adaptive courses and games (e.g., CTQ, GidgetML), chatbot support (ScratchThAI), AR authoring (ExposAR), and ML-integrated programming environments, but does not report pooled effect sizes or aggregate sample sizes.
findings.measure: Reported benefits for computational thinking education across reviewed studies

findings.finding_summary: The review found that AI-supported CT initiatives were frequently associated with increased motivation, engagement, and opportunities for creative/project-based learning, including learning in informal spaces and collaborative settings. Examples include gamified platforms, museum-based games, and project-based programming/ML activities, though no pooled quantitative estimates were provided.
findings.measure: Motivation, engagement, and CT-related skill practice across reviewed studies

findings.finding_summary: The review identified challenges alongside benefits, including the difficulty of accurately characterizing students' CT competencies for adaptive systems, the expertise required to develop and sustain AI-based CT tools, and concerns that over-reliance on AI may diminish students' creativity and innovation. These findings are synthesized qualitatively from the included studies and are not accompanied by pooled quantitative estimates.
findings.measure: Reported challenges and risks of AI use in computational thinking education

quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic literature review synthesizing heterogeneous higher-education AI-in-CT studies, but it does not provide meta-analytic effect sizes, pooled quantitative estimates, or a formal risk-of-bias synthesis. The evidence is therefore review-based but primarily qualitative and mixed in rigor.
impact_tier_rationale: The review reports generally positive and some mixed findings, but impact magnitude is unclear because no pooled effect sizes or consistent quantitative outcome measures are reported.
